notes: Layers run from the centre outward. outerKm is the outer radius of the layer; fraction = outerKm / mean radius (public/data/solar/bodies.json).
outerRangeKm / fractionRange give the spread of published models; model: true marks values that depend on an interior model rather than a direct measurement.
Temperatures inside every body are model estimates except Earth's inner-core boundary (iron melting experiments) and the Sun's photosphere (observed).
provenance: observed = measured directly (seismology, helioseismology); derived = computed from measurements (gravity, moment of inertia, induction); model = model-dependent.

bodies.name: Sun
bodies.lede: A ball of hot plasma that makes its own light. Energy made in the core takes over 100,000 years to reach the surface.

howWeKnow.text: Millions of sound waves ring the Sun. Their frequencies, measured from Doppler shifts at the surface, map sound speed and rotation with depth. They put the base of the convection zone at 0.713 of the radius.
Neutrinos escape the core directly. Detectors such as Borexino count the ones from fusion, confirming the core temperature the models predict.

layers.name: Core
layers.composition: Hydrogen fusing into helium (about two-thirds helium by mass at the centre)
layers.plain: Where the Sun's energy is made. Every second about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen fuse into helium here.

layers.name: Radiative zone
layers.plain: Energy creeps outward as light that is absorbed and re-emitted again and again. This random walk is what makes the journey so slow.

layers.name: Tachocline
layers.plain: A thin shear layer where the solidly rotating interior meets the convection zone, whose equator spins faster than its poles. It is thought to help drive the Sun's magnetic cycle.

layers.name: Convection zone
layers.plain: Here the gas boils. Hot plumes rise, cool and sink, carrying energy to the surface in about a week to a month.

layers.name: Photosphere
layers.composition: Hydrogen and helium; the layer that emits the light we see
layers.plain: The visible surface, about 500 km deep. Its effective temperature is 5772 K. The granules are the tops of convection cells.

bodies.name: Mercury
bodies.lede: A small planet with a giant metal core that fills about 83% of its radius.

howWeKnow.text: MESSENGER tracked how Mercury's gravity pulls on the spacecraft and how much the planet wobbles (librates). Together they give the moment of inertia and the size of the core.
Mercury has a weak global magnetic field, so part of its core must still be liquid metal.

layers.name: Solid inner core
layers.plain: Gravity data from MESSENGER show a solid inner core, but its exact size is still uncertain.

layers.name: Liquid outer core
layers.plain: Swirling liquid metal makes Mercury's magnetic field.

layers.name: Mantle
layers.plain: A thin rocky mantle, only about 380 km thick.

layers.name: Crust
layers.plain: About 35 km thick on average (models span 17 to 53 km).

bodies.name: Venus
bodies.lede: Earth's near twin in size. No spacecraft has measured its interior directly, so its layers come from models.

howWeKnow.text: Radar echoes from Earth timed Venus's slow spin and wobble, giving the first moment of inertia (0.337 ± 0.024). It implies an iron core about 3500 km in radius, with large uncertainty.
Magellan mapped gravity and topography. Comparing them constrains the thickness of the crust.

bodies.uncertainty: Model-based: Venus has no seismic or detailed tidal data yet. Whether its core is liquid or has a solid inner part is unknown.

layers.name: Iron core
layers.plain: Probably similar to Earth's core, but Venus has no magnetic field, so the core may not be convecting.

layers.name: Mantle
layers.plain: A rocky mantle like Earth's. Hot plumes may still rise through it and feed volcanoes.

layers.name: Crust
layers.plain: Basalt crust about 8 to 50 km thick. The surface itself is 740 K, hot enough to melt lead.

bodies.name: Earth
bodies.lede: The best-known interior in the universe, mapped by the earthquake waves that pass through it.

howWeKnow.text: Earthquake waves speed up, slow down and bend at each boundary. S waves cannot cross the liquid outer core, which casts a shadow on the far side of the planet. PREM is the reference model built from these travel times.
Laboratory experiments squeeze iron to core pressures. The melting point at the inner-core boundary gives its temperature, about 6200 K.

layers.name: Inner core
layers.plain: A ball of solid metal as hot as the Sun's surface. It stays solid because the pressure is over 3 million times that at the surface.

layers.name: Outer core
layers.plain: Flowing liquid metal. Its currents generate Earth's magnetic field.

layers.name: D″ layer
layers.plain: The bottom few hundred km of the mantle, where heat flows out of the core.

layers.name: Lower mantle
layers.plain: Solid rock that still creeps a few centimetres a year, slowly stirring the planet.

layers.name: Upper mantle
layers.plain: The tectonic plates ride on its softer upper part, the asthenosphere.

layers.name: Crust
layers.plain: The thin rocky skin we live on: 5 to 10 km under the oceans and 30 to 70 km under the continents.

bodies.name: Moon
bodies.lede: Apollo seismometers still tell us about the Moon's small iron core, decades after the astronauts left.

howWeKnow.text: Apollo astronauts left seismometers that recorded moonquakes until 1977. Reprocessed records reveal reflections from a solid inner core and a liquid outer core.
The twin GRAIL spacecraft mapped the Moon's gravity in detail, giving the crust's thickness and density.

layers.name: Solid inner core
layers.plain: A ball of iron about 480 km across. A 2023 study combining gravity and laser ranging found a similar size.

layers.name: Liquid outer core
layers.plain: Still partly molten, but no longer strong enough to make a magnetic field.

layers.name: Partially molten layer
layers.composition: Silicate rock with a little melt
layers.plain: A slushy layer at the base of the mantle.

layers.name: Mantle
layers.plain: Solid rock. The dark maria on the near side are lava that rose from it billions of years ago.

layers.name: Crust
layers.plain: On average 34 to 43 km thick, thicker on the far side.

bodies.name: Mars
bodies.lede: InSight listened to marsquakes for four years and measured the crust and core of another planet for the first time.

howWeKnow.text: Marsquake waves reflected off the crust layers and the core. The first analysis put the core edge at 1830 km.
Waves that crossed the core showed a molten rock layer about 150 km thick sitting on top of it. The liquid iron core is then smaller, about 1650 km, and denser.

layers.name: Liquid core
layers.composition: Iron with sulfur, oxygen, carbon and hydrogen
layers.plain: Liquid iron rich in lighter elements. With no dynamo today, Mars lost its global magnetic field long ago.

layers.name: Molten silicate layer
layers.plain: A layer of melted rock wrapped around the core. In 2021 its top was taken to be the core's surface.

layers.name: Mantle
layers.plain: Solid rock that fed giant volcanoes such as Olympus Mons.

layers.name: Crust
layers.plain: Between 24 and 72 km thick on average, measured from marsquake echoes.

bodies.name: Jupiter
bodies.lede: No solid surface: the gas gets denser with depth until hydrogen turns into a liquid metal. Juno found the core is fuzzy, not a hard ball.

howWeKnow.text: Juno measured tiny ripples in Jupiter's gravity. Only models with heavy elements spread through a large dilute core fit them.
Experiments and quantum simulations show that hydrogen becomes an electrical conductor at about 1 to 2 million times Earth's air pressure.

layers.name: Dilute core
layers.composition: Rock and ice dissolved in metallic hydrogen
layers.plain: Heavy elements spread out over up to half or more of the radius instead of sitting in a small rocky ball.

layers.name: Metallic hydrogen
layers.plain: Hydrogen squeezed until it conducts electricity like a metal. Its flow powers the strongest magnetic field of any planet.

layers.name: Molecular envelope
layers.composition: Molecular hydrogen and helium, with ammonia and water clouds near the top
layers.plain: The outer layer, whose colourful cloud bands are all we can see.

bodies.name: Saturn
bodies.lede: Saturn's rings act as a seismometer: waves inside the planet tug on ring particles and reveal a large diffuse core.

howWeKnow.text: Oscillations inside Saturn shift its gravity slightly. Cassini saw the patterns they carve into the C ring.
Cassini dived between the planet and the rings in 2017 and measured the gravity field precisely.

layers.name: Diffuse core
layers.composition: Rock and ice (about 17 Earth masses) mixed with hydrogen and helium
layers.plain: A gradual mix of heavy elements that reaches about 60% of the way out.

layers.name: Metallic hydrogen
layers.composition: Hydrogen and helium; helium may rain out here
layers.plain: A shell of metallic hydrogen generates Saturn's magnetic field.

layers.name: Molecular envelope
layers.composition: Molecular hydrogen and helium with ammonia clouds
layers.plain: Saturn is so light overall that it would float in a big enough bath of water.

bodies.name: Uranus
bodies.lede: An ice giant: most of its mass is a hot, dense fluid of water, ammonia and methane, not frozen ice.

howWeKnow.text: Only Voyager 2 has visited, in 1986. Its gravity data and ring-orbit precession allow many interior models.
The field is tilted and off-centre, so it is likely made in a thin conducting shell of ionic water, not a deep core.

bodies.uncertainty: Layer boundaries differ widely between models; the layers may also blend gradually.

layers.name: Rocky core
layers.plain: A rocky centre perhaps the size of Earth or smaller.

layers.name: Icy mantle
layers.plain: The "ices" are hot fluids under enormous pressure. Water may even become superionic.

layers.name: Hydrogen-helium envelope
layers.composition: Hydrogen, helium and methane (the methane gives the cyan colour)
layers.plain: A deep atmosphere that blends into the icy mantle below.

bodies.name: Neptune
bodies.lede: Uranus's near twin in size, but with a hot interior that drives the fastest winds in the Solar System.

howWeKnow.text: Voyager 2 flew past in 1989. Its gravity data, with the planet's shape, constrain models of the layers.

bodies.uncertainty: Layer boundaries differ widely between models; the layers may also blend gradually.

layers.name: Rocky core
layers.plain: A rocky centre perhaps about Earth's size.

layers.name: Icy mantle
layers.plain: Most of Neptune's mass is this hot, electrically conducting fluid, which makes its magnetic field.

layers.name: Hydrogen-helium envelope
layers.plain: Methane absorbs red light and gives Neptune its blue colour.

bodies.name: Ceres
bodies.lede: The largest body in the asteroid belt has a muddy, salty interior with pockets of brine.

howWeKnow.text: Dawn orbited Ceres from 2015 to 2018. Its gravity field shows a light crust over a denser, water-rich rocky mantle.
Salts in Occator crater came up from a deep brine reservoir.

layers.name: Rocky mantle
layers.composition: Hydrated rock with salty brine near the top
layers.plain: Rock altered by water. A layer of brine may still sit at its top.

layers.name: Crust
layers.plain: About 41 km thick and lighter than rock: a frozen mix of ice, salts and clay.

bodies.name: Pluto
bodies.lede: Beneath Pluto's nitrogen glaciers there is probably an ocean of liquid water.

howWeKnow.text: Pluto's size and mass give a mean density of 1854 kg/m³: about two-thirds rock and one-third ice.
The giant ice-filled basin sits almost exactly opposite Charon. That is easiest to explain if a dense ocean lies beneath it.

bodies.uncertainty: The ocean is inferred, not observed directly; its thickness is a model estimate.

layers.name: Rocky core
layers.plain: A rocky core about 1700 km across.

layers.name: Subsurface ocean
layers.plain: An ocean perhaps more than 100 km deep, kept liquid by heat from the rocky core.

layers.name: Ice shell
layers.composition: Water ice under nitrogen, methane and carbon monoxide ices
layers.plain: A thick shell of water ice, hard as rock at −230 °C.

bodies.name: Io
bodies.lede: The most volcanic world known. Tides from Jupiter knead its interior and keep it hot.

howWeKnow.text: Galileo's flybys showed an iron core and a rocky mantle.
Galileo saw a magnetic signal suggesting a partly molten layer. In 2024 Juno measured how much Io flexes and ruled out a shallow, fully liquid magma ocean.

layers.name: Iron core
layers.plain: Its size depends on how much sulfur it holds: 650 km for pure iron, 950 km for iron sulfide.

layers.name: Mantle
layers.plain: Hot rock heated by tides, not by radioactivity alone.

layers.name: Partially molten layer
layers.plain: Rock with pockets of magma that feed more than 400 active volcanoes.

layers.name: Crust
layers.plain: A rigid lid a few tens of km thick, constantly resurfaced by lava.

bodies.name: Europa
bodies.lede: A global ocean with about twice the water of all Earth's oceans lies under Europa's ice.

howWeKnow.text: Galileo's flybys showed a dense centre and a water layer about 80 to 170 km thick on top.
Jupiter's changing field induces a magnetic signal in Europa. Only a salty, electrically conducting ocean explains it.

layers.name: Iron core
layers.plain: A metal core probably 800 to 1400 km across.

layers.name: Rocky mantle
layers.plain: If the seafloor is volcanically active, it could supply chemical energy for life.

layers.name: Ocean
layers.plain: Perhaps about 100 km deep, ten times deeper than Earth's deepest trench.

layers.name: Ice shell
layers.plain: Probably more than 20 km thick (estimates range from a few km to about 40 km).

bodies.name: Ganymede
bodies.lede: The largest moon in the Solar System is the only one with its own magnetic field, and it hides a salty ocean.

howWeKnow.text: Galileo found that Ganymede is fully separated into layers and makes its own magnetic field, so it has a liquid iron core.
Ganymede's aurorae rock back and forth less than expected. A salty ocean under the ice dampens the motion.

layers.name: Iron core
layers.plain: A liquid metal core that makes the moon's own magnetic field.

layers.name: Rocky mantle
layers.plain: A rocky layer under hundreds of km of water and ice.

layers.name: High-pressure ice
layers.composition: Dense ice phases (ice V and VI)
layers.plain: Ice so compressed that it is denser than water and sinks.

layers.name: Ocean
layers.plain: A salty ocean sandwiched between two layers of ice.

layers.name: Ice shell
layers.plain: An outer shell of ordinary ice about 150 km thick.

bodies.name: Callisto
bodies.lede: Callisto's rock and ice never fully separated, yet it may still hide a thin ocean.

howWeKnow.text: Callisto's moment of inertia, 0.355, is too high for a fully layered body: rock and ice are only partly separated.
Galileo detected an induced magnetic signal consistent with a salty ocean, though Callisto's ionosphere may contribute too.

bodies.uncertainty: The ocean is debated, and the boundary between the rock-ice interior and the ice is gradual.

layers.name: Rock-ice interior
layers.composition: Mixed rock and ice, rockier towards the centre
layers.plain: A mixture of rock and ice that only partly separated.

layers.name: Possible ocean
layers.plain: A layer of salty water could exist here. It is not certain.

layers.name: Ice shell
layers.plain: An ancient, heavily cratered crust of ice more than 100 km thick.

bodies.name: Enceladus
bodies.lede: A small moon with a global ocean that sprays out into space through cracks at its south pole.

howWeKnow.text: Cassini flybys showed a light rocky core and dense water beneath the south pole.
Enceladus wobbles too much for its ice to be attached to the core. The ice must float on a global ocean.

layers.name: Porous rocky core
layers.plain: A loose, water-filled rocky core where tides create heat.

layers.name: Ocean
layers.composition: Salty water with silica, hydrogen and organic molecules
layers.plain: Cassini flew through the plumes and tasted salts, silica and organic molecules from this ocean.

layers.name: Ice shell
layers.plain: About 20 km thick on average, but only a few km at the south pole where the jets erupt.

bodies.name: Titan
bodies.lede: Titan has rain and lakes of methane on top and a salty water ocean below.

howWeKnow.text: Titan's moment of inertia, about 0.34, shows rock and ice only partly separated.
Saturn's pull raises tides on Titan about 10 m high, far more than solid ice allows. A liquid ocean must lie under the ice.

layers.name: Rocky core
layers.plain: A rock core that may still contain water in its minerals.

layers.name: High-pressure ice
layers.plain: Dense ice sitting on the rock core.

layers.name: Ocean
layers.composition: Water, possibly with ammonia and salts
layers.plain: A deep ocean, possibly very salty.

layers.name: Ice shell
layers.composition: Water ice under a thick nitrogen atmosphere
layers.plain: An ice shell about 50 to 200 km thick. The surface is 94 K.
